distribution: Worldwide; common in greenhouse and field-grown tomatoes

leaves: Older leaves develop brown, scorched margins that curl upward and inward
Distinct border between brown and green tissue, often with a thin yellow line
Systemic infections can cause leaf wilting and firing (browning and collapse)
stems: Light streaks develop that darken and split forming shallow cankers
Vascular tissue discolored yellow to tan, pith may become reddish-brown and mealy or hollow
Branches may break off easily in advanced infections
fruit: Raised, white blisters on green or red fruit (‘bird's eye’ spots), 1/16–1/8 inch (3–4 mm) in diameter
Fruit near calyx may have brown seeds due to vascular invasion
seedlings: Poor growth, temporary wilting, lower leaves yellow and shrivel
Symptoms often appear at flowering or later

disease_cycle: Introduced via infected seed or transplants
Survives in infested plant residue for up to 3 years; can survive on contaminated benches, stakes, and weed hosts
Spread by windblown rain, sprinkler irrigation, mechanical cultivation, and handling
Bacteria enter seedlings through wounds, broken trichomes, or leaf cuts, then move systemically through xylem

prevention: Use disease-free seeds and transplants; certified seeds recommended
Soak seeds in 130°F water for 25 minutes to reduce contamination
Steam or disinfect greenhouse flats, benches, and potting media
Rotate crops out of tomatoes for at least one season
cultural: Incorporate plant debris thoroughly at season end
Control nightshade weeds that may harbor bacteria
Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet
Minimize overhead irrigation and handle plants carefully to reduce wounding
chemical: Copper bactericides may reduce spread during wet conditions, but do not control systemic infections
Disinfect tools and surfaces with 0.5–1% calcium or sodium hypochlorite, or commercial disinfectants like Physan

notes: Economic losses are usually minor in direct-seeded fields unless wet conditions favor secondary spread
Greenhouse transplants are more vulnerable; vigilance in sanitation is critical
Even a few infected seeds can result in high levels of infected transplants
references: Jones, J.B., et al. 2014. Compendium of Tomato Diseases and Pests, 2nd Edition. APS Press.
University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources. Tomato Pest Management Guidelines: Bacterial Canker.
Schaad, N.W., et al. 2001. Bacterial Cankers of Tomato. Plant Health Progress.
